title: StateFlow & SharedFlow mechanics
scopeHtml: Scope: the mechanics of MutableStateFlow and MutableSharedFlow (initial value, conflation, equality, atomic updates, replay/buffer/overflow config, emit vs tryEmit, read-only exposure). Facts verified against kotlinx.coroutines 1.4+ behavior (StateFlow/SharedFlow stable since 1.4.0, update {} since 1.5.1). LiveData comparison and one-off-event design live in the next chunk.

notes.title: StateFlow basics and initial value
notes.html:
The idea. A StateFlow is a whiteboard that always shows ONE current value. Anyone who looks at it sees the latest value immediately, and anyone watching gets told when the value changes. It never is "empty": you must give it a starting value.

Mechanism. MutableStateFlow<T>(initial) is a hot flow: it exists and holds its value whether or not anyone collects. It has a .value property you can read and write from any thread (reads and writes are thread-safe). A new collector first receives the current value, then every later change. A StateFlow never completes: collect on it never returns normally, it only stops when the collecting coroutine is cancelled. That is why you collect it inside launch and never put code after collect expecting it to run.

class CartViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _count = MutableStateFlow(0)       // initial value is mandatory
    val count: StateFlow<Int> = _count
    fun add() { _count.value = _count.value + 1 }  // see "Atomic updates": this is racy
}

Real examples. Jetpack Compose screens usually do val state by vm.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle(); the initial value is what the first frame draws (a loading state). Swiggy/Zomato-style screens model Loading | Content | Error as a sealed UiState inside one StateFlow. Google's "Now in Android" sample exposes StateFlow<UiState> from every ViewModel.

Everyday picture. The scoreboard at a cricket ground: it always shows the current score, even if you walk in late; you never see "no score".

Common interview traps.

  • Believing StateFlow can be created without an initial value (it cannot; use null/Loading as the first state or a SharedFlow).
  • Writing code after collect on a StateFlow and expecting it to run.
  • Thinking .value is "cold": it is the live current value, readable without collecting.

notes.title: Read-only exposure with asStateFlow
notes.html:
The idea. Keep the pen inside the ViewModel; show the UI only a glass window. Outsiders may look at the state but must not write it.

Mechanism. Hold a private MutableStateFlow and expose it as StateFlow (an upcast, so callers cannot call .value = ). asStateFlow() goes one step further: it wraps the flow in a ReadonlyStateFlow object, so even a cast (flow as MutableStateFlow) fails. asSharedFlow() does the same for SharedFlow. The wrapper has near-zero cost.

private val _state = MutableStateFlow(UiState())
val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state.asStateFlow()

Real examples. The Android architecture guide, Now in Android and most Hilt ViewModels use the _state / state pair. It enforces unidirectional data flow: UI sends events down to the ViewModel, state flows up.

Everyday picture. A shop display window: customers see the items, only staff can rearrange them.

Common interview traps.

  • Exposing MutableStateFlow publicly so any Composable/Fragment can mutate state.
  • Thinking a plain upcast is airtight: a as MutableStateFlow cast works on it, asStateFlow() blocks that.
  • Forgetting that the backing field name _state is only a convention, not a language feature.

notes.title: Conflation and equality in StateFlow
notes.html:
The idea. A StateFlow only cares about the LATEST value, and it ignores a "change" that is not a change. If the board shows 5 and you write 5 again, nobody is notified. If you write 1, 2, 3 very fast, a slow reader may only see 3.

Mechanism. Two behaviours:

  1. Equality dedupe. Setting value compares the new value to the old with equals(). If equal, nothing is emitted (this is built in, like distinctUntilChanged). For data classes this is structural equality; for plain classes it is reference equality.
  2. Conflation. StateFlow holds one slot. If a collector is slow, intermediate values are overwritten; the collector gets the newest on its next turn. It never queues.
data class UiState(val items: List<Item> = emptyList())
state.value = UiState(listOf(a))     // emitted
state.value = UiState(listOf(a))     // equal data class: NOT emitted

Production patterns. (a) Mutating a list in place (list.add(x); _state.value = list) never fires because it is the same reference and equal to itself: classic "UI doesn't update" bug. Always copy: _state.value = _state.value.copy(items = items + x). (b) A data class with a field that is a lambda or an array: arrays use reference equality, so you may get spurious or missed updates. (c) For a design that wants dedupe (a screen state), StateFlow is right; for a design that wants every write delivered (a "retry clicked" signal where the same value must re-trigger), StateFlow is wrong and you should use SharedFlow/Channel.

Everyday picture. A lift's floor indicator: pressing the already-lit floor button does nothing, and if five people press buttons while it moves, the display only shows where it is now.

Common interview traps.

  • Mutating a mutable collection held in state and expecting a UI update.
  • Expecting every intermediate value to reach a slow collector.
  • Putting a field in a state class that has no meaningful equals (arrays, Bitmap) and getting wrong dedupe.
  • Using StateFlow for something that must re-fire with the same value.

notes.title: Atomic updates with update
notes.html:
The idea. value = value + 1 is "read, think, write": two threads can both read 5 and both write 6, losing one increment. Like two people updating a shared spreadsheet cell from stale copies.

Mechanism. MutableStateFlow.update { old -> new } runs a compare-and-set loop (compareAndSet(expect, new)) and retries if someone else changed the value in between. Your lambda must therefore be pure and cheap, because it can run more than once. Variants: updateAndGet, getAndUpdate. compareAndSet itself uses equals, so equal-but-different-instance values can behave slightly surprisingly.

_state.update { it.copy(count = it.count + 1) }   // safe from any thread

Inside update do not do side effects (network, logging, analytics.track): a retry would repeat them.

Real examples. A Paytm-like cart updated by a button tap and a background sync at the same moment; two viewModelScope.launch blocks both calling _state.value = _state.value.copy(...) and silently overwriting each other's field (a flaky "my loading flag stuck on" bug that is hard to reproduce).

Everyday picture. Two clerks editing the same paper ledger line: update is "check the line still says what I read before I overwrite it".

Common interview traps.

  • Using value = value.copy(...) from multiple coroutines.
  • Putting side effects in the update lambda.
  • Thinking update locks: it is lock-free CAS with retry, not a mutex.

notes.title: SharedFlow configuration: replay and buffer
notes.html:
The idea. A SharedFlow is a radio broadcast: whoever is tuned in hears it. Unlike StateFlow it has no "current value" and no required initial value. You tune it with three knobs: replay, extraBufferCapacity, onBufferOverflow.

Mechanism.

  • replay = n: the last n emitted values are kept and handed to each NEW subscriber. Default 0 = latecomers hear nothing from the past.
  • extraBufferCapacity = m: extra slots on top of replay so emitters can push without waiting for slow collectors.
  • onBufferOverflow: what to do when buffer (replay + extra) is full: SUSPEND (default; emitter waits for the slowest subscriber), DROP_OLDEST, DROP_LATEST. The two DROP options require buffer size greater than 0 (replay or extra at least 1), otherwise the constructor throws.
val events = MutableSharedFlow<Event>(
    replay = 0,
    extraBufferCapacity = 64,
    onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST
)

MutableSharedFlow() with defaults has zero buffer: emit suspends until every current subscriber has received the value, and with NO subscribers, the value is simply lost.

Scale 10x thinking. If traffic grows (a price ticker, location, socket messages), the default SUSPEND makes one slow subscriber stall the producer and therefore all other subscribers. Choose: bigger extraBufferCapacity (memory grows, each slot holds an object), DROP_OLDEST for "latest wins" data (prices, location), or a per-subscriber .buffer()/.conflate() so slowness is isolated. Never leave an unbounded growth path: SharedFlow buffers are bounded, which is a feature.

Real examples. WhatsApp-like socket message bus with DROP_OLDEST for typing indicators and a larger buffer with SUSPEND for actual messages; Zerodha/Groww-style price ticks use DROP_OLDEST since stale ticks are worthless; an app-wide "session expired" event bus with replay 0.

Everyday picture. A school PA announcement: if you were out of the room you missed it (replay 0); if the loudspeaker waits for the slowest listener to nod, the whole school waits (SUSPEND).

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting a default MutableSharedFlow() to remember values for late collectors.
  • Using DROP_OLDEST/DROP_LATEST with zero buffer (throws IllegalArgumentException).
  • Forgetting one slow subscriber can stall the emitter under SUSPEND.
  • Treating extraBufferCapacity as per-subscriber: it is shared buffer.

notes.title: emit versus tryEmit
notes.html:
The idea. emit is "hand over and wait if needed" (a suspend function, polite). tryEmit is "try to drop it in; tell me if it did not fit" (non-suspending, returns Boolean).

Mechanism. emit suspends when the buffer is full and overflow is SUSPEND. tryEmit never suspends: it returns true if accepted, false if it would have had to suspend. With DROP_OLDEST/DROP_LATEST, tryEmit always returns true (it can always make room or discard). With a default zero-buffer SharedFlow and active subscribers, tryEmit returns false because there is nowhere to put the value; with no subscribers it returns true (value discarded, as there is nobody to deliver to). StateFlow's tryEmit always succeeds (it just sets the value).

Spot-the-bug.

private val _clicks = MutableSharedFlow<Unit>()      // zero buffer
fun onClick() { _clicks.tryEmit(Unit) }              // BUG: returns false, click lost

Fixes: add extraBufferCapacity = 1, or use viewModelScope.launch { _clicks.emit(Unit) }, or use a Channel. The silent false is why this is a production bug: nothing throws, the button just "sometimes doesn't work" under load. tryEmit is what you use from non-suspend callbacks (View listeners, Java callbacks, callbackFlow bridges) and that is exactly where you must size the buffer.

Real examples. Bridging a LocationCallback or a click listener into a SharedFlow; in a non-suspend onLocationResult use tryEmit with a DROP_OLDEST buffer.

Everyday picture. Posting a letter: emit waits at the counter until the clerk is free; tryEmit drops it in the box and walks away, and if the box is full, the letter bounces back to your hand and you may not notice.

Common interview traps.

  • Ignoring the Boolean result of tryEmit.
  • Calling emit from a non-coroutine callback (compile error) and "fixing" it with runBlocking on the main thread (ANR).
  • Assuming tryEmit on a default MutableSharedFlow always works.

notes.title: Subscription timing and subscriptionCount
notes.html:
The idea. A SharedFlow with no replay only delivers to those listening AT THE MOMENT of emission. If you emit before the collector starts, it is gone. This is the root of "my event got lost on screen rotation".

Mechanism. Each collector registers a subscriber slot; subscriptionCount is a StateFlow<Int> of current subscribers. Emission with zero subscribers drops the value (for replay 0). Collector start is asynchronous: scope.launch { flow.collect {} } does not guarantee the collector is registered before the next line runs (it depends on the dispatcher; Dispatchers.Main.immediate or CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED get you there synchronously). This causes the classic test flake: emit right after launch { collect } and the first value is missed. Tests with Turbine or UnconfinedTestDispatcher avoid it.

subscriptionCount is also how shareIn(started = WhileSubscribed) knows when to start/stop the upstream, and you can use sharedFlow.subscriptionCount.first { it > 0 } to wait for a listener before emitting.

Production incident pattern. A ViewModel emits "navigate to Home" from init {} after a quick cached login check; the Fragment collects in onViewCreated slightly later. No subscribers at emission time, event dropped, the user sits on a blank splash. Another: during rotation the Fragment is destroyed (collector cancelled) and the event emitted in that gap is lost. Remedies: replay-and-clear semantics (Channel), or model it as state that the UI consumes and acknowledges.

Everyday picture. A train announcement: if you were buying tea at the moment it was made, you never hear it, and nobody repeats it.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing launch { collect } has already subscribed when launch returns.
  • Emitting important signals during init of a ViewModel into replay-0 SharedFlow.
  • Not knowing subscriptionCount exists or what it is used for.

notes.title: StateFlow versus SharedFlow with replay 1
notes.html:
The idea. "SharedFlow with replay = 1" looks like StateFlow (new listeners get the last value) but is not the same thing.

StateFlow SharedFlow(replay=1)
Initial value required none (can be empty)
.value property yes no (use replayCache.firstOrNull())
Equality dedupe yes (equals) no, every emit is delivered
Conflation always only with DROP_OLDEST
Never completes yes yes
Delivers same value twice no yes

StateFlow is effectively MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1, onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST) plus distinctUntilChanged plus a mandatory initial value plus .value.

Ambiguous requirement. "Show the last known value to new screens and also let me re-trigger identical values": that is SharedFlow(replay=1), because a "refresh" with the same data must still go through. "Show current screen state": StateFlow. A cached user profile that is rarely updated: StateFlow. A "reload" signal where tapping twice should fire twice: not StateFlow.

Migrating a SharedFlow to StateFlow under live traffic. Steps that work: (1) find every consumer that relied on duplicate emissions or on "no initial value" (those break); (2) add an explicit initial/Loading state and a sealed representation of "nothing yet"; (3) keep the old public SharedFlow API temporarily, implemented as stateFlow.drop(1) or .asSharedFlow() bridges, and roll out consumers one by one; (4) check tests relying on first() hanging vs returning immediately, since StateFlow returns the initial value instantly. Watch for events modelled as state, which now get deduped and silently drop repeated identical events.

Everyday picture. A notice board (StateFlow) shows the current notice and does nothing if you pin the same notice again; a WhatsApp group (SharedFlow replay 1) repeats the last message to new joiners and shows every message you send, duplicates included.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying they are identical because both replay one value.
  • Forgetting StateFlow dedupes: two identical "ShowToast" objects collapse into one.
  • Migrating without handling the new mandatory initial value.

notes.title: Internals and replay cache
notes.html:
The idea. Under the hood both are small arrays of values plus a list of "where is each reader up to".

Mechanism (senior depth). Both extend AbstractSharedFlow<S>, which keeps an array of slots, one per subscriber (SharedFlowSlot / StateFlowSlot), and a nCollectors counter. SharedFlowImpl has a circular buffer (buffer: Array<Any?>) with indices replayIndex, minCollectorIndex, bufferSize, queueSize; the slowest subscriber's position (minCollectorIndex) determines how much must be retained, which is why one slow collector can block SUSPEND emitters. Emitters that cannot fit are queued as Emitter objects and resumed when the slowest collector moves on.

StateFlowImpl is much simpler: an atomic _state field holding the value (or a NULL sentinel) plus a version counter sequence. Each StateFlowSlot is a tiny state machine (NONE / PENDING / a suspended continuation). A write bumps the sequence, and each collector wakes up, reads the latest value, and compares to the last one it saw (equals), which is the conflation and dedupe mechanism. That is also why StateFlow can not queue values.

replayCache and resetReplayCache. sharedFlow.replayCache returns a snapshot List<T> of currently replayed values (at most replay of them). It is a snapshot, not live. MutableSharedFlow.resetReplayCache() clears the replay buffer so new subscribers get nothing from the past; it only works as intended when you want to "forget" (e.g. user logged out, so the cached user object must not be replayed to the next screen). On a MutableStateFlow, resetReplayCache() throws UnsupportedOperationException because StateFlow must always have a value.

Production incident: stale replay. A MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1) kept "last Order object". After logout and a different user logging in, the new Orders screen briefly displayed the previous user's order because the replay cache survived (a privacy bug!). Fix: call resetReplayCache() on logout, or scope the flow to the session component (Hilt @SessionScoped-like custom component), not an app singleton. Another: replay > 1 with a big payload keeping hundreds of Bitmaps/list copies alive in memory: a leak that looks like a ViewModel leak in LeakCanary because the singleton holds references.

Everyday picture. A circular conveyor sushi belt with a marker per diner showing how far each has eaten; the chef cannot clear a plate until the slowest diner has passed it.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling resetReplayCache() on a StateFlow.
  • Treating replayCache as a live view.
  • Leaving user data in a replay cache of a singleton across logouts.
  • Using large replay values, which pins memory.

notes.title: Operators on shared flows
notes.html:
The idea. A shared flow is hot and never ends, so ordinary operators behave in surprising ways on it.

Mechanism. Operators like map, filter work, but they return a plain cold Flow, not a SharedFlow/StateFlow: you lose .value, .replayCache, and the hotness (each collector re-runs the operator). Terminal operators like toList(), first(), last() on a never-ending shared flow either never return or only return after a condition; toList() hangs forever. distinctUntilChanged() on a StateFlow is redundant (and, since Kotlin coroutines 1.6-ish, flagged as deprecated/error-level via @Deprecated "applying distinctUntilChanged to StateFlow has no effect"). Applying conflate(), .buffer() or flowOn to a shared flow similarly has no effect on the shared part ("shared flows are already conflated/buffered; flowOn has no effect" is documented behaviour, and SharedFlow.flowOn is deprecated-warned). To convert back into state use stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000), initial); to share a cold flow use shareIn.

Multi-flow consistency (post-incident). Collecting two StateFlows separately, launch { a.collect(::renderA) }; launch { b.collect(::renderB) }, lets the UI show a new A with an old B for a moment (a "torn" state: price updated but currency not, or a Pay button enabled while the form is invalid). Fix: one StateFlow of a combined immutable UiState, or combine(a, b) { ... }.stateIn(...) in the ViewModel, so the UI always renders a consistent pair. Keep derived values derived (computed in combine), not stored twice.

Real examples. Search screens combine queryFlow + filtersFlow into results; Compose screens collect exactly one state; Spotify-like players combine playbackState and currentTrack before the UI sees them.

Everyday picture. Two clocks in a station that are updated by two separate staff members: for a minute they disagree; one clock showing both times in a single display cannot disagree.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling toList() or last() on a StateFlow/SharedFlow and hanging forever.
  • Expecting map on a StateFlow to still have .value.
  • Applying distinctUntilChanged to StateFlow (redundant) or flowOn to shared flows (ineffective).
  • Collecting several state flows separately and rendering them as if they were one consistent snapshot.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• StateFlow = hot, always has a value, equals dedupe, conflated, never completes; read with .value, expose with asStateFlow().
  • Update state with update {} (atomic CAS loop, pure lambda), never value = value.copy() from several coroutines; never mutate a collection in place.
  • SharedFlow = hot broadcast with replay, extraBufferCapacity, onBufferOverflow; defaults have no memory, and SUSPEND lets the slowest subscriber stall everyone.
  • emit suspends, tryEmit returns Boolean and silently fails on a full zero-buffer flow; subscriptionCount tells you who is listening.
  • Events emitted when nobody collects are lost in replay-0 flows; StateFlow is not SharedFlow(replay=1): it dedupes and needs an initial value.
  • Internals: SharedFlow has a circular buffer driven by the slowest collector; StateFlow is one atomic value plus a sequence; clear leaked data with resetReplayCache() (not on StateFlow).
  • Operators on shared flows return cold flows and lose state features; combine related flows into one state to avoid torn UI.

questions.promptHtml: What is a StateFlow, how does it differ from a regular cold Flow, and what are the rules you must know before using MutableStateFlow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every modern ViewModel exposes a StateFlow. They want to see whether you understand it as "an observable variable" and not "a flow you collect once".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A StateFlow is a hot flow that always holds exactly one current value. It needs an initial value, .value reads it without suspending, every new collector immediately receives the current value, and it conflates: a slow collector only ever sees the latest value, and setting a value equal to the current one does nothing. It never completes, so collect never returns normally. A cold Flow has no state and re-runs its producer for each collector; a StateFlow has one shared state and no producer."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A cold flow {} is a recipe: each collect runs the block from scratch. StateFlow<T> is the opposite: the state exists independently of collectors.

 writers                         readers
 _state.value = x  ----->  [ StateFlowImpl: one value ]  -----> collector A (own slot)
 _state.update{..} ----->        (version / equals)      -----> collector B (own slot)
                                                         -----> .value (plain read)

Rules:

  1. Initial value is mandatory: MutableStateFlow(initial). There is no "empty" StateFlow. If "not loaded yet" is a real state, model it (Loading, or T? with null).
  2. .value is a synchronous, thread-safe read/write. Writing never suspends. emit() and tryEmit() on a MutableStateFlow are just the value setter (tryEmit always returns true).
  3. A new collector gets the current value first, then later changes. replayCache is always a single-element list with the current value.
  4. Conflation + equality dedupe: a collector sees the latest value, not every value; writing a value equals to the current one is ignored (details in Q516).
  5. Never completes: collect on a StateFlow has return type Nothing. Code after it in the same coroutine is unreachable. Collection ends only by cancelling the collecting coroutine. Operators like toList() on a StateFlow hang forever.
  6. subscriptionCount is itself a StateFlow<Int>.
  7. StateFlow has no error channel: it cannot "fail". Failures must be modelled as state.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class CounterViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _count = MutableStateFlow(0)          // initial value required
    val count: StateFlow<Int> = _count.asStateFlow()  // read-only exposure

    fun inc() { _count.update { it + 1 } }            // atomic read-modify-write
}

// Broken expectation: this never prints "done"
viewModelScope.launch {
    vm.count.collect { println(it) }
    println("done")   // unreachable; collect returns Nothing
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating StateFlow as an event stream: duplicates are swallowed and fast sequences are conflated.
  • Calling first()/take(n) is fine, but toList() or collect {} followed by code is a hang/dead code.
  • Using null as "not loaded" and then forgetting that StateFlow<T?> forces null checks everywhere; a sealed UI state is cleaner.
  • Assuming .value inside a coroutine is always the same as what a collector last saw. The collector may lag behind.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why no suspending emit semantics? → Because there is always room: the buffer is the single value slot; setting just overwrites it.
  2. Is StateFlow thread-safe? → Yes for value, update, compareAndSet. Your own read-then-write on .value is not atomic (see Q517).
  3. Can a StateFlow hold null? → Yes if T is nullable; initial null is a valid state.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE answer: "it's like LiveData for flows". The senior answer lists the semantic contract (one slot, equality dedupe, conflation, never completes, Nothing collect) and names which of those contract pieces will break a feature (events, counters, analytics).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A screen "stopped updating" because someone wrote collect {} and then a second launch-less statement after it; the second part never ran. Review catches this once you know collect is Nothing on shared flows.

questions.promptHtml: Why do we write private val _state = MutableStateFlow(...) and val state: StateFlow<...> = _state.asStateFlow()? What does asStateFlow() actually do, and what's the difference between that and just declaring the type as StateFlow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Encapsulation of state ownership is the core of unidirectional data flow. The follow-up probes whether you know a plain upcast is not a real barrier.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The ViewModel must be the only writer. I keep the mutable one private and expose a read-only type. asStateFlow() returns a wrapper that delegates to the original but is not a MutableStateFlow, so even a cast fails at runtime. Just declaring val state: StateFlow<X> = _state is only a compile-time restriction; anyone can do state as MutableStateFlow<X> and write to it. The same applies to asSharedFlow()."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
MutableStateFlow<T> : StateFlow<T>, MutableSharedFlow<T>. An upcast keeps the same object, so a downcast succeeds. asStateFlow() is implemented as ReadonlyStateFlow(this, null), a class that implements only StateFlow<T> and forwards value, replayCache, collect. The cast as MutableStateFlow throws ClassCastException.

Practical reasons for the private/public pair:

  • Single writer: all state transitions live in one class, so you can reason about and test them.
  • Binary/API stability: exposing StateFlow lets you change internals (e.g. replace MutableStateFlow with stateIn(...) of a combined flow) without touching callers.
  • Kotlin trick: Kotlin has no "public read, private write" for property types, hence the backing-property convention (_state). The explicit type also prevents the inferred public type from becoming MutableStateFlow.

Cost: one small wrapper allocation per property, once. Negligible.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class VM : ViewModel() {
    private val _ui = MutableStateFlow(UiState())
    val ui: StateFlow<UiState> = _ui.asStateFlow()   // wrapper, cast-proof

    val leaky: StateFlow<UiState> = _ui              // compile-time only
}

(vm.leaky as MutableStateFlow<UiState>).value = UiState() // compiles and works (bad)
(vm.ui as MutableStateFlow<UiState>)                       // ClassCastException

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Exposing MutableStateFlow publicly "just for the test". Use Turbine/a fake instead.
  • Believing asStateFlow() makes a snapshot copy. It is a live view; it still reflects every change.
  • Naming: _state for the mutable backing field is convention, not syntax. Detekt/ktlint rules often enforce it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does asSharedFlow() do the same for SharedFlow? → Yes, ReadonlySharedFlow, same idea.
  2. Does stateIn() need this pair? → No. stateIn already returns a read-only StateFlow; there is no mutable handle.
  3. Should the collector ever get MutableStateFlow to write back (two-way binding)? → Prefer an event/function (onQueryChanged(q)) so the ViewModel remains the sole writer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "so the UI can't modify it". The senior adds: the plain upcast is not enforcement, asStateFlow() is, and the pair is about preserving the freedom to change implementation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "temporary" public MutableStateFlow in a repository was written from three screens; a bug where a stale screen reset shared state took a day to find because writes were untraceable.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the three parameters of MutableSharedFlow(replay, extraBufferCapacity, onBufferOverflow): what each does, what the defaults are, and what the default MutableSharedFlow() actually does.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: SharedFlow misconfiguration (usually the default) causes silently lost events. This is the single most common SharedFlow interview question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "replay is how many past values a new subscriber gets. extraBufferCapacity is extra buffer space beyond replay for slow subscribers. onBufferOverflow decides what happens when that buffer is full: SUSPEND (default), DROP_OLDEST, or DROP_LATEST. Defaults are 0, 0, SUSPEND. So MutableSharedFlow() has no buffer: with no subscribers an emitted value is simply dropped, and with subscribers emit suspends until every one of them has received it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Total buffer = replay + extraBufferCapacity. The replay part is kept even without subscribers (it's the replay cache). The extra part is used only while there are subscribers who haven't consumed yet.

Config Behavior
MutableSharedFlow() rendezvous: emit suspends until all current subscribers take the value; no subscribers -> value dropped
replay = 1 new subscriber gets last value; buffer size 1; slow subscriber suspends emitter when full (SUSPEND)
extraBufferCapacity = 64 emitter can run 64 ahead of slowest subscriber, then suspends
onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST emitter never suspends; slow subscriber skips older values (needs total buffer >= 1)
onBufferOverflow = DROP_LATEST emitter never suspends; new value discarded when buffer full

Constraints: replay >= 0, extraBufferCapacity >= 0; a non-SUSPEND overflow strategy with replay == 0 && extraBufferCapacity == 0 throws IllegalArgumentException (there is no buffer to drop from). replay + extra must not overflow Int.

Semantics worth stating:

  • All subscribers see all values (unlike StateFlow's conflation) unless you chose a DROP strategy and a subscriber is slower than the buffer.
  • With SUSPEND, the slowest subscriber governs the emitter: one stuck collector blocks emit for everybody (see the firehose scenario).
  • Zero subscribers + any strategy: the value only goes into the replay cache (size replay); it never suspends.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val a = MutableSharedFlow<Int>()                         // 0,0,SUSPEND
val b = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(replay = 1)               // late subscribers get last
val c = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(
    extraBufferCapacity = 64,
    onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST        // fire-and-forget, never suspends
)
// MutableSharedFlow<Int>(onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) // IllegalArgumentException

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Emitting into a default SharedFlow before the collector has started: the value is lost.
  • Choosing replay to "make it not lose events" and then replaying stale events to every new subscriber.
  • Forgetting that DROP_OLDEST/LATEST make tryEmit always succeed (good), but data does get dropped (document that).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What's replayCache? → Read-only snapshot list of values a new subscriber would get.
  2. Difference between replay=1 and extraBufferCapacity=1? → Replay re-delivers to new subscribers; extra buffer only helps existing slow ones.
  3. Can the buffer be unlimited? → There is no UNLIMITED for SharedFlow (that's Channel); you can set a huge capacity but you then own the OOM risk.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE can name the parameters. Senior states the defaults, the "slowest subscriber governs emitter" rule, the no-subscriber drop, and picks the config from the use case (events vs state vs firehose).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An analytics bus built on MutableSharedFlow() lost the first screen-view events after cold start since the logger collector attached ~200 ms after the first emits.

questions.promptHtml: StateFlow is described as "conflated" and "distinct-until-changed". What exactly does that mean, when can a collector miss a value, and what breaks if your state class has a weird equals?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The classic "I set the state and the UI didn't update" bug lives here.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Writing to MutableStateFlow.value compares the new value to the current one using equals. If equal, nothing happens, no emission, no version bump. Separately, each collector only sees the latest value at the time it resumes, so if you set A, B, C quickly, a slow collector may see only C. Also A then back to A before the collector wakes up means it sees nothing. So correctness depends on your state having a correct equals; data classes are fine; mutating an object in place and re-assigning the same reference does nothing."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
StateFlowImpl.updateState(expectedState, newState) runs under a lock: if oldState == newState (equals) it returns true without changing anything. Otherwise it stores the new value, bumps an internal sequence, and marks every collector's slot "pending" (resuming ones that were suspended).

Each collector runs roughly:

loop:
  v = state.value
  if (v != lastEmittedToThisCollector) { downstream.emit(v); lastEmitted = v }
  await slot pending flag   // suspends until some writer sets it

Consequences:

  • Conflation: the collector reads value when it runs, not the sequence of intermediate writes. 10 writes while it was busy -> it sees the last.
  • A->B->A before collector runs: when it wakes, value == lastEmitted -> skip. It never knows anything happened.
  • Dispatcher delay: collectors on Dispatchers.Main get dispatched via a handler post; writes between post and execution are conflated even though the collector is "fast".
  • Equality quality:
    • data class: structural equals, good.
    • plain class without equals: identity equality -> every new instance emits (more recomposition, but no lost updates).
    • class with incorrect equals (ignores a field): changes to that field are silently swallowed.
    • Same mutable object (e.g. MutableList) mutated and reassigned: old == new is the same reference -> no emission.
    • Array-typed properties in a data class: arrays use reference equality inside equals, so equal contents may re-emit, or different arrays with the same ref don't.
    • Floating point: Double.NaN/-0.0 semantics follow equals, not ==.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val s = MutableStateFlow(UiState(items = emptyList()))
s.value = UiState(items = emptyList())        // equals -> ignored

val list = mutableListOf(1)
val m = MutableStateFlow(list)
list.add(2)
m.value = list                                // same reference, equals -> NOT emitted (bug)
m.value = list.toList()                       // new instance, different contents -> emitted

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mutable collections inside state (the next chunk covers the full "list mutation" story).
  • Putting System.currentTimeMillis() or a request-id in state purely to "force" emission, which pollutes the model; instead ask why you need a re-emit (Q523).
  • Expecting every state transition to reach analytics/test assertions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to observe every value anyway? → Use SharedFlow with buffer, or log at the producer.
  2. Does collectLatest or conflate matter on StateFlow? → No, it's already conflated by design (Q526).
  3. Does equality compare deeply? → It calls equals; deep only if your classes' equals is deep (List.equals is structural, arrays are not).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer: "it ignores same values". The senior explains where the comparison happens, the A-B-A case, dispatcher-induced conflation, and the equals pitfalls (identity, arrays, partial equals).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cart badge never updated for one SKU variant because the equals override excluded a quantity field to dedupe diffing.

questions.promptHtml: Why is _state.value = _state.value.copy(x = ...) considered unsafe, and how do update {}, getAndUpdate, updateAndGet and compareAndSet fix it? What rules must the lambda follow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Lost updates in shared state are a top race condition on Android. They look for CAS understanding and the "lambda may run more than once" rule.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "value is thread-safe for a single read or write, but read-then-write is two operations. Two coroutines can both read count=5 and both write 6, losing an update. update {} runs a compare-and-set loop: read current, compute next from your lambda, compareAndSet(current, next), retry if someone else changed it in the meantime. The lambda must be pure and fast because it can run several times."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The standard implementation:

inline fun <T> MutableStateFlow<T>.update(function: (T) -> T) {
    while (true) {
        val prevValue = value
        val nextValue = function(prevValue)
        if (compareAndSet(prevValue, nextValue)) return
    }
}

compareAndSet(expect, update) is atomic and compares with equals (not identity). Careful corner case documented by the library: if both expect and update equal the current value, it returns true but doesn't change the stored reference.

 T1: read 5 --------- compute 6 --- CAS(5->6) ok
 T2:        read 5 --- compute 6 ------------ CAS(5->6) FAILS (current is already 6) -> retry: read 6, compute 7, CAS ok

Variants: getAndUpdate returns the previous value, updateAndGet the new one. Available since 1.5.1.

Lambda rules:

  1. Pure: no I/O, analytics, Toast, no launch. It may run N times under contention.
  2. Cheap: heavy work inside lengthens the window and raises retry count (livelock-ish under contention). Compute expensive things outside, pass results in.
  3. Derive only from it, not from a stale outer copy of state.
  4. Don't read other mutable state non-atomically inside (that read can be inconsistent).

When you need "decide + side effect": use getAndUpdate (or update and then compare), perform the side effect once, outside:

val old = _state.getAndUpdate { it.copy(submitting = true) }
if (!old.submitting) startSubmit()   // exactly one winner

Note: this is also the idiom for "exactly once" guard against double taps.

Single-writer case: if all writes happen on viewModelScope (Main.immediate), .value = .value.copy() is race-free in practice, since there is no interleaving between read and write without a suspension point. Don't write code whose correctness depends on that; use update always, it costs nothing.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken under concurrency: lost updates
_cart.value = _cart.value.copy(qty = _cart.value.qty + 1)

// Correct
_cart.update { it.copy(qty = it.qty + 1) }

// Broken: side effect in lambda runs >1 time on contention
_cart.update { analytics.log("inc"); it.copy(qty = it.qty + 1) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing val s = _state.value; ...suspend call...; _state.value = s.copy(...): a stale snapshot overwrites changes made during the suspension, even single-threaded.
  • Using Mutex around .value writes: unnecessary.
  • Assuming update is a lock; it is lock-free optimistic.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can update livelock? → In theory under extreme contention with expensive lambdas; in practice no; keep lambdas tiny.
  2. compareAndSet uses == or ===? → equals.
  3. How do you make multi-field state consistent? → One immutable state object, one update; separate StateFlows can't be updated atomically together (see Q530).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use update". Senior explains the CAS loop, the re-execution rule, the stale-snapshot-across-suspension bug even on one thread, and the getAndUpdate once-only guard.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Order quantity totals drifted 1-2% for users who tapped "+" quickly on a screen whose mutations ran in Dispatchers.Default; update fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: What's the difference between emit and tryEmit on MutableSharedFlow, when does tryEmit return false, and why does tryEmit on a default MutableSharedFlow() seem to "not work"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Calling from callbacks (non-suspending contexts) is everyday Android; people hit this and blame the library.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "emit is suspending: it waits if the buffer is full. tryEmit never suspends and returns a Boolean: true if the value was accepted, false if it would have needed to suspend. On a default SharedFlow with no buffer and SUSPEND overflow, there's never room, so with subscribers present tryEmit returns false and the value is dropped; with no subscribers it returns true but the value is lost anyway because nobody is listening and replay is 0. Add extraBufferCapacity or a DROP overflow policy, and tryEmit works from callbacks."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Internal logic (simplified from SharedFlowImpl):

tryEmit(v):
  if no collectors: store only in replay cache (size replay) -> true
  else if buffer full (bufferSize >= replay + extra) and slowest collector hasn't consumed:
      SUSPEND     -> return false
      DROP_LATEST -> drop v, return true
      DROP_OLDEST -> drop oldest, add v, return true
  else add to buffer -> true

emit(v): if (tryEmit(v)) return else suspend (queue emitter) until space

Cases:

Config subscribers? tryEmit
default (0,0,SUSPEND) none true, value dropped
default >=1 false (rendezvous needs suspension)
extra=N SUSPEND >=1 true until N unconsumed, then false
any with DROP_* any always true
replay=1 none true, kept in replay cache

emit on the default flow with subscribers does work (rendezvous: it suspends until collectors take it), which is why code using emit in a coroutine "works" and then breaks when someone changes it to tryEmit in a callback.

Also: tryEmit is non-blocking and thread-safe (guarded by a lock). MutableStateFlow.tryEmit always returns true.

Choosing: callback APIs (click listeners, sensor, BroadcastReceiver) -> tryEmit with a buffer and DROP_OLDEST (or callbackFlow / trySend channel). Coroutine context where you need guaranteed delivery and can wait -> emit with SUSPEND.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: default config + tryEmit from a callback
private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<Event>()
fun onClick() { _events.tryEmit(Event.Clicked) }   // false when collectors exist

// Fixed
private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<Event>(
    extraBufferCapacity = 16,
    onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST
)
fun onClick() { check(_events.tryEmit(Event.Clicked)) }  // always true here

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Ignoring the Boolean result. At minimum assert/log in debug.
  • "Fixing" by viewModelScope.launch { _events.emit(x) } for each callback: ordering is no longer guaranteed across launches on multi-threaded dispatchers.
  • Using runBlocking { emit } in callbacks: ANR risk.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does emit with no subscribers not suspend? → There is no one to wait for; value goes to the replay cache and returns.
  2. Is there trySendBlocking-style for SharedFlow? → No. Use a Channel for blocking handoff.
  3. Does DROP_LATEST return true even when it dropped? → Yes; the call "succeeded" under that policy. You can't tell it was dropped.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "tryEmit is non-suspending". Senior gives the truth table, explains why default+tryEmit silently fails, and picks the buffering policy deliberately.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A permission-result callback used tryEmit on a default SharedFlow; the "granted" event vanished whenever the collector was already attached (tryEmit returned false), while a different timing with no collector lost it silently as well. Both paths dropped it, which made the bug look flaky.

questions.contextHtml:
A fitness app (1.2M DAU) wraps a vendor BLE heart-rate SDK. The SDK calls onSample(bpm: Int) on its own binder thread about 1 Hz. A new ViewModel was written like this, and QA reports "the BPM tile stays at -- on Pixel 7 and Galaxy S23; it works on one old test phone". No crash, no logs.

class HrViewModel(private val sdk: HrSdk) : ViewModel() {
    private val _samples = MutableSharedFlow<Int>()
    val samples: SharedFlow<Int> = _samples

    init {
        sdk.setListener { bpm -> _samples.tryEmit(bpm) }
        sdk.start()
    }
}

// Fragment
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        vm.samples.collect { tile.text = it.toString() }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug(s), explain exactly why it fails on some devices, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Probably threading, post to main." or "Use emit instead." The first misses that SharedFlow is thread-safe; the second can't be done in a non-suspending callback without extra machinery and doesn't address the missing first value or replay.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the tile need the last known value after rotation or when the screen returns to STARTED (so replay)? Can samples be dropped (1 Hz, only latest matters)? Does the SDK deliver before the screen is visible? Does the old phone start the SDK later than the collector attaches?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: give the flow a buffer so tryEmit can succeed: MutableSharedFlow<Int>(replay = 1, onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST). That's a one-line patch behind the current release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) tryEmit returning false with the default config (rendezvous, collector attached); (b) values emitted before the collector attaches are dropped (no replay, and repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) re-subscribes, so anything emitted while stopped is lost); (c) main-thread issue (red herring: collect runs on lifecycleScope, i.e. Main.immediate; emission thread is irrelevant); (d) SDK not delivering (red herring on devices where it works).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the return value of tryEmit: Log.d("HR", "tryEmit=${..}"). On the failing devices it prints false once the collector is attached, true before (then lost). A unit test with UnconfinedTestDispatcher and Turbine reproduces: tryEmit on default flow with an active collector returns false.
  5. Root cause: Default MutableSharedFlow() has zero buffer with SUSPEND overflow. tryEmit cannot suspend, so with a subscriber it returns false and drops the value; with no subscriber it returns true but the value is discarded (replay = 0). The "works on one old phone" report is timing luck (for example the tile was filled from a different path there); I'd say plainly that I can't prove why that phone differs without its logs, but the loss itself is deterministic for this config, not device-specific.
  6. Fix: Short-term: the replay=1 + DROP_OLDEST config above, and check the Boolean in debug. Long-term: this is state (current BPM), so use MutableStateFlow<Int?>(null) with _bpm.value = bpm, which is non-suspending, thread-safe, and replays the latest to returning screens.
private val _bpm = MutableStateFlow<Int?>(null)
val bpm: StateFlow<Int?> = _bpm.asStateFlow()
sdk.setListener { _bpm.value = it }
  1. Prevention: Lint/detekt rule or code-review checklist item: "no tryEmit on a MutableSharedFlow without buffer/drop policy; unused Boolean results from tryEmit flagged". Unit test that emits from a plain thread while a Turbine collector is active.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't wrap in viewModelScope.launch { emit } per sample (unbounded coroutine creation, ordering not guaranteed on multithreaded dispatchers). I wouldn't use Channel(UNLIMITED) for a 1 Hz sample: memory risk and one-shot consumption semantics.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if samples must never be dropped (medical logging)? → Then it's a stream, not state: Channel(UNLIMITED) or a callbackFlow/buffer(Int.MAX) into a persisted store; handle backpressure by writing to Room.
  • Why not DROP_LATEST? → Latest reading is the most valuable; DROP_LATEST keeps stale data.
  • Does MutableStateFlow.tryEmit have this issue? → No, it always returns true.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team shipped a sensor wrapper with a default SharedFlow and tryEmit; it passed instrumented tests because the test collector was attached late and used emit. The first production report arrived two weeks later from a single OEM. The fix was one line; the investigation cost days because nothing logged the Boolean.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames threads or says "use LiveData" without identifying tryEmit/buffer semantics.
  • Hire: Identifies default config + tryEmit returning false, fixes with buffer or DROP_OLDEST.
  • Strong hire: Also explains the lost-before-subscribe case, recognises it's state not events and moves to StateFlow, and adds prevention (return-value check, test, review rule).

questions.promptHtml: I call emit on a MutableSharedFlow right after launching a collector, and the collector sometimes misses the first value. Why, and what are subscriptionCount and onSubscription for?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Hot flows have no memory unless you give them one. This tests the mental model and test-writing skills.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A SharedFlow without replay delivers a value only to subscribers that exist at the moment of emission. launch { flow.collect {} } returns immediately; the coroutine hasn't necessarily started collecting yet, so an emit right after can happen before the subscription exists, and it's dropped. To coordinate, subscriptionCount is a StateFlow of the number of active collectors (you can first { it > 0 } before emitting), and onSubscription { } runs an action after the collector is registered, guaranteeing it won't miss what follows. Or give the flow replay."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Subscription happens when collect begins executing and registers a slot. With a regular launch on a dispatcher, the start is a dispatch, so there is a gap.

main:      launch{collect} ----> emit(1) ----------------------------> 
collector:                    (queued) ... starts, subscribes ... collect(2)
                                 ^ emit(1) dropped (replay=0, no subscribers)

Tools:

  • CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED / Dispatchers.Main.immediate/UnconfinedTestDispatcher: the collector runs until its first suspension synchronously, so it has subscribed by the time launch returns. Common in tests, not a design guarantee in production.
  • sharedFlow.subscriptionCount: StateFlow<Int>; emitter can subscriptionCount.first { it > 0 } then emit. Useful for "start the producer only when someone listens" (but see SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed for the managed way).
  • sharedFlow.onSubscription { emit(x) }: the lambda executes after the subscription is registered; anything emitted by others after that point is received. Typical usage: emit an initial snapshot first, then live updates, without a gap.
  • replay = n: new subscribers receive up to n recent values, which removes the race for "current value" use cases but also replays stale data.

Gotcha: subscriptionCount counts collectors currently collecting; with repeatOnLifecycle it drops to 0 when the UI is stopped. Values emitted then are lost without replay/buffer.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val events = MutableSharedFlow<Int>()

val job = scope.launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) {
    events.collect { println("got $it") }
}
events.emit(1)    // received: collector already subscribed

// Explicit coordination
launch {
    events.subscriptionCount.first { it > 0 }
    events.emit(2)
}

// Gap-free snapshot + live
events.onSubscription { emit(currentSnapshot()) }.collect { render(it) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Tests that pass because runTest's UnconfinedTestDispatcher/backgroundScope happened to subscribe eagerly, while production dispatchers do not.
  • delay(100) "to let the collector attach".
  • Using subscriptionCount as a lock: it can change right after you read it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does StateFlow have this problem? → No, a late collector receives the current value.
  2. Is onSubscription the same as onStart? → onStart runs before the upstream collection starts, onSubscription runs after the shared-flow subscription is established; only the latter closes the gap.
  3. How do you test SharedFlow emissions deterministically? → Turbine's test {} starts collecting before you act (it uses an unconfined collector), or UnconfinedTestDispatcher for the collector.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use replay". Senior distinguishes start-undispatched, onSubscription and subscriptionCount, and explains why replay can be wrong (stale replays).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A deep-link event emitted from onCreate was lost because the collector lived in a fragment that subscribed 2 frames later.

questions.contextHtml: A checkout ViewModel exposes StateFlow<PaymentState> with states Idle -> Authorizing -> Verifying3DS -> Capturing -> Success. The repository's local mock path updates these synchronously; the real path updates them with 50-400 ms between. Product analytics shows funnel steps Verifying3DS and Capturing logged for only 62% of successful payments, while server logs show every payment went through all steps. A PM says "analytics is dropping events, fix the SDK". The analytics call is inside viewModel.state.collect { analytics.track(it) } on Main. About 380k payments/day.
questions.promptHtml: Is the analytics SDK dropping events? What's going on and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the analytics SDK buffer / add retry." This keeps blaming the sink and ignores that the source never delivered those values to that collector.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which states are missing, only fast ones? Does the missing rate correlate with device speed or network speed? Where does the tracker collect (Main, with what lifecycle)? Do we need exactly-once per transition, or "at least once"? What does the UI need from these states?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed for users; this is data quality. Annotate the dashboard as unreliable for those steps so decisions aren't made on it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) StateFlow conflation: the collector resumes on Main later than two state writes, so it reads the last one only; (b) collector is under repeatOnLifecycle and the app was backgrounded during 3DS, so transitions happened while stopped; (c) analytics SDK dropping (red herring, the SDK logs show it received only what we sent); (d) equal states deduplicated (e.g. Capturing twice).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log in the producer vs in the collector with a correlation id and compare counts. Add a temporary counter of value writes per payment. Reproduce with a unit test: write three states in a row without suspension and Turbine-collect; observe only the last (with unconfined collector all three show, so also test with a standard dispatcher).
  5. Root cause: StateFlow represents "the current state", not "every transition". The collector is dispatched on Main and by the time it runs, intermediate values were overwritten. Correlation with fast paths (cached responses, 3DS frictionless) matches 62%.
  6. Fix: Track transitions where they happen, in the state machine that performs them: call analytics.track(PaymentStep.X) from the ViewModel/use case when the transition is made (once per transition, with the payment id), not by observing a state holder. If we really need a stream of transitions, expose a separate SharedFlow<PaymentStep>(extraBufferCapacity = 64); the UI continues to use StateFlow.
private fun transition(next: PaymentState) {
    _state.value = next
    analytics.track(next.toStep())     // at the source, exactly once per transition
}
  1. Prevention: A team rule: "State is for rendering. Anything that must see every transition or must fire once is not collected from a StateFlow." Add a unit test per state machine that asserts the analytics call sequence, not the flow collection.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't add yield()/delay(1) between state writes to let collectors keep up (hides, adds latency, still not guaranteed). I wouldn't switch the whole screen to SharedFlow(replay=1) (loses dedupe and initial value semantics).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the UI also must show a 300 ms spinner for each step? → That's a presentation requirement; model it in the UI layer (minimum display time), not by relying on lack of conflation.
  • What if tracking at the source duplicates on config change replay? → It's in the ViewModel's transition function, which runs once per actual transition regardless of collectors.
  • How would you see all values in a test? → Turbine with UnconfinedTestDispatcher, but remember this makes tests more permissive than production.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A funnel dashboard showed a mysterious 30-40% drop between two steps that only existed on fast devices. The team spent a sprint tuning network code before someone noticed the collector-based tracker was losing steps; moving the call to the transition function "fixed" a conversion rate that had never changed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the SDK or adds retries.
  • Hire: Identifies conflation and moves tracking to the source or a SharedFlow.
  • Strong hire: Also separates state from events as a principle, validates via producer-vs-collector counts, considers lifecycle gaps and test permissiveness.

questions.promptHtml: MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1, onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST) looks like a StateFlow. What are the actual differences, and when would you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you know StateFlow's specific guarantees rather than treating it as a SharedFlow alias.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "They look similar but differ in four ways: StateFlow requires an initial value and has .value; StateFlow ignores writes equal to the current value, SharedFlow delivers every emission including duplicates; StateFlow's replayCache can't be reset, SharedFlow's can; and StateFlow always has a value to hand to new collectors, while the SharedFlow variant has none until the first emit. I use StateFlow for state, SharedFlow for events or when I need duplicates, no initial value, or resetReplayCache."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect MutableStateFlow(x) MutableSharedFlow(replay=1, DROP_OLDEST)
Initial value required none; replay cache empty
Synchronous read .value replayCache.lastOrNull() (snapshot, may be null)
Equal consecutive values ignored (distinct) delivered again
Slow collector sees latest only (conflated) buffer size 1 + DROP_OLDEST: also latest only; with larger replay/extra it can see more
Atomic read-modify-write update, compareAndSet none (replayCache read then emit is racy)
emit/tryEmit emit never suspends; tryEmit always true never suspends, tryEmit true
resetReplayCache() throws UnsupportedOperationException clears cache
Collector gets value on collect always (one value) only if cache non-empty
Implementation specialized StateFlowImpl (single slot per collector, very light) general SharedFlowImpl (circular buffer, queue)
stateIn / shareIn result type StateFlow SharedFlow
Compose collectAsStateWithLifecycle needs initial; StateFlow gives it requires explicit initialValue

Behavior example: emitting 1, 1, 1:

  • StateFlow(initial 0): collectors receive 0, 1 (once).
  • SharedFlow(replay=1): collectors receive 1, 1, 1.

When to pick which:

  • UI state, "current value" semantics, derived .value reads, atomic updates -> StateFlow.
  • Repeated identical occurrences are meaningful (a "refresh" tick, a repeated retry tap) or you want "no value yet" without a sentinel -> SharedFlow. But for UI events, see the next chunk on one-off events.
  • Need to wipe cached data at logout -> SharedFlow(replay=1) + resetReplayCache() or a StateFlow whose value is a sentinel Empty.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val st = MutableStateFlow(0)
val sh = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(replay = 1, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)

launch { st.collect { println("st $it") } }
launch { sh.collect { println("sh $it") } }
yield()
repeat(3) { st.value = 1; sh.emit(1) }
// st 0, st 1     |   sh 1, sh 1, sh 1
// st.resetReplayCache()  // UnsupportedOperationException

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Emulating StateFlow with SharedFlow and then reading replayCache.first() (throws if empty) in "synchronous" code.
  • Racing sh.emit(sh.replayCache.last().copy()): not atomic; StateFlow has update.
  • Assuming a SharedFlow with replay=1 equals "new collector gets latest once": it also replays the stale value on every resubscription, e.g. after repeatOnLifecycle restarts.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does StateFlow's conflation depend on equality only? → There are two layers: equality dedupe on write, and "latest value on read" per collector.
  2. Is MutableStateFlow also a MutableSharedFlow? → Yes, MutableStateFlow<T> : StateFlow<T>, MutableSharedFlow<T>, so you can pass it where a MutableSharedFlow is expected, with StateFlow semantics.
  3. Which is cheaper? → StateFlow: one array of slots and a version; no buffer. In practice irrelevant unless thousands.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "StateFlow has a value". Senior produces the full difference table, notes the atomic-update and reset differences, and ties choice to semantics (state vs occurrences).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team replaced StateFlow with SharedFlow(replay=1) "to allow null" and silently started re-rendering and re-logging on every identical emit (see migration scenario Q529).

questions.contextHtml: A stock-watch screen (900k DAU) shows a quote list. A QuoteRepository polls every 5 s and the ViewModel does _ui.value = UiState(quotes = repo.fetch()). During market closure, quotes are identical, so the UI shows no change; support is flooded with "app is frozen, data is not refreshing". Design adds a "Last updated 12:03:15" label and pull-to-refresh which must show the spinner for the duration of a manual fetch. A junior proposes: "StateFlow ignores equal values. Let's make UiState non-data class (identity equals) so every fetch re-emits."
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate the proposal and design the state so users get correct feedback.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Either accepts the identity-equals hack, or says "add a timestamp field to force a change" without explaining why that is (and isn't) the same thing.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is "last updated" a user-facing fact (then it is state)? Should a failed refresh show something different from "market closed"? How much does re-composition/re-render cost with 200 rows? Is the poll in the foreground only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship lastSyncedAt in the state; no model hack.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The "frozen" perception is a missing-information problem, not an emission problem: data identical is legit. Re-emitting would cause re-render and flicker for no new information.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compose recomposition counts (Layout Inspector), a quick count of emissions per minute in market-closed hours; usability test: with lastSyncedAt ticking, do "frozen" tickets drop?
  5. Root cause: _ui.value = same is correctly deduped. The user needs the fact that a sync happened, which is information; make it part of state.
  6. Fix:
data class UiState(
    val quotes: List<Quote> = emptyList(),
    val lastSyncedAt: Instant? = null,
    val isRefreshing: Boolean = false,
    val syncError: SyncError? = null,
)

private fun poll() = viewModelScope.launch {
    while (isActive) {
        runCatching { repo.fetch() }
            .onSuccess { q -> _ui.update { it.copy(quotes = q, lastSyncedAt = clock.now(), syncError = null) } }
            .onFailure { e -> if (e is CancellationException) throw e
                         _ui.update { it.copy(syncError = e.toSyncError()) } }
        delay(5_000)
    }
}

isRefreshing toggled true/false by manual refresh via update. Because lastSyncedAt changes, emission is legitimate every 5 s; the Compose list uses stable keys and the quotes list is equals-equal, so items do not recompose (skipped via structural equality/stability). 7. Prevention: Principle: if the UI should react, it must be a state difference; never fight the dedupe. Add a unit test: identical fetch -> state changes only in lastSyncedAt. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't use identity-equals (breaks copy-based diffing, causes full re-renders at 12 emits/min over 900k users and fails when two non-equal things should compare equal). I wouldn't append a random nonce to the state. I'd consider emitting lastSyncedAt through its own flow if the clock label is far cheaper to render than the list, to avoid re-composing the list container; Compose's skipping handles this for stable inputs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the refresh must trigger a side effect like a haptic even with equal data? → That's an event; use a one-off mechanism (next chunk) with an explicit event type, not state.
  • The label should say "5 s ago" ticking each second? → Derive in the UI from lastSyncedAt with a ticker local to the composable; don't push ticks through the ViewModel state.
  • Does List<Quote> equals cost matter? → O(n) per write; with 200 items trivial, with 50k use a persistentList or version number, but measure first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "force emit" hack (random UUID in state) shipped for a similar screen; it caused full list re-layout every poll and a measurable battery regression, then a second bug when UUID made the Compose previews differ in screenshot tests.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adopts identity-equality or random field hack uncritically.
  • Hire: Explains dedupe is correct, adds explicit lastSyncedAt/isRefreshing state.
  • Strong hire: Distinguishes state vs event, handles error state, recomposition cost, and cancellation correctness in the loop.

questions.promptHtml: How do StateFlowImpl and SharedFlowImpl work internally? What explains conflation in one and per-subscriber delivery and backpressure in the other?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Staff-level signal: can you reason from mechanism, e.g. predict who suspends when, memory behavior, and what "slow subscriber" costs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "StateFlow keeps one atomic value plus a version and one tiny slot per collector; a write bumps the version and wakes each slot, and each collector re-reads the value, so intermediates are naturally skipped. SharedFlow keeps a circular buffer with indices: replay window, the position of the slowest subscriber, and a queue of suspended emitters; each subscriber has a slot with its own read index. The buffer entries can be freed only after the slowest subscriber has passed them, which is why one slow subscriber blocks the emitter under SUSPEND."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
(Implementation details; names from the open-source code, may change between versions but behavior is documented.)

StateFlowImpl

_state: atomic holder of (value, sequence)   guarded by `synchronized(this)` for writes
slots:  array of StateFlowSlot, one per active collector
StateFlowSlot._state: NONE | PENDING | continuation(suspended collector)

write(new):
  lock { if (old == new) return;  value = new;  sequence++ ; 
         for each slot: slot.makePending()  // resumes suspended collectors }
collector loop:
  oldState = null
  while (true) {
     newState = flow.value
     if (oldState == null || oldState != newState) { collector.emit(newState); oldState = newState }
     if (!slot.takePending()) slot.awaitPending()   // suspend until a write marks pending
  }

Memory: O(1) value + O(collectors). No buffer, no queue. Writes never suspend.

SharedFlowImpl

buffer: Array<Any?> (circular)          bufferSize, queueSize
replayIndex  : index of first replayed item
minCollectorIndex : smallest read index among active subscribers
head = min(minCollectorIndex, replayIndex)   // oldest retained item
slots: per-subscriber SharedFlowSlot { index, continuation }
emitters waiting: stored in the same buffer beyond bufferCapacity as `Emitter` nodes (queueSize)
  • Subscribe: slot.index = replayIndex (so they see the replay window first).
  • tryEmit: if buffer has room (bufferSize < replay + extra) or there are no subscribers, append; otherwise by policy: SUSPEND -> false (emit then enqueues an Emitter and suspends); DROP_OLDEST -> advance head, append; DROP_LATEST -> discard.
  • After an append, resume subscribers suspended waiting for new items.
  • When a subscriber moves its index, minCollectorIndex updates; entries older than min(minCollectorIndex, replayIndex) are cleared and queued emitters promoted, resuming them.
  • Cost: emit is O(1) amortized plus waking up subscribers: O(subscribers) per emit. Each subscriber's collect loop takes the next item at its index, calls downstream.emit (which may suspend while the collector body runs), and loops.

Resulting behavior:

  • StateFlow conflates because collectors read "the latest" rather than "the next".
  • SharedFlow delivers sequentially because collectors read "the next at my index".
  • SUSPEND backpressure = emitter queued behind the slowest subscriber's read index; under DROP_OLDEST the head advances regardless, and a slow subscriber's index is bumped forward to the new head (it skips values silently).
  • Memory ceiling = (replay + extra) elements + queued emitters (each with a continuation). Unbounded queued emitters are possible if many coroutines call emit concurrently against a stuck subscriber with SUSPEND; each is a suspended coroutine holding its value: a leak vector.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Observable consequence of "read next at my index"
val sh = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(extraBufferCapacity = 2)
launch { sh.collect { delay(100); println("slow $it") } }
launch { sh.collect { println("fast $it") } }
repeat(5) { sh.emit(it) }  // once the 2-slot buffer fills behind the slow reader, emit suspends

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking SharedFlow "broadcasts" values like callbacks; actually emit waits for the slowest under SUSPEND.
  • Thinking each subscriber has its own buffer; the buffer is shared, with per-subscriber indices.
  • Treating internals as API.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can subscriptionCount be a StateFlow? → The impl keeps a MutableStateFlow<Int> updated on slot allocate/free.
  2. What happens to a subscriber's slot on cancellation? → It's freed; minCollectorIndex recomputed, which may release queued emitters.
  3. What's the worst-case behavior with 10k concurrent emitters? → 10k suspended emitters in the queue with their payloads; memory and wakeup cost, so cap emitters or use DROP.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "StateFlow conflates, SharedFlow doesn't". Senior describes read-latest vs read-next, shared buffer with per-subscriber index, and derives the slowest-subscriber blocking and memory ceilings from it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A log bus with SUSPEND and 20 concurrent producers piled up 50k suspended emitters behind a stalled disk-writing subscriber and drove an OOM; DROP_OLDEST bounded it.

questions.contextHtml: A banking-lite app (2.4M MAU) has a @Singleton ProfileRepository exposing val profile: SharedFlow<Profile> backed by MutableSharedFlow<Profile>(replay = 1). Screens collect it. After a rollout, security gets a report: after logging out and logging in as a different user (shared family tablet), the Home screen briefly (~300-900 ms) shows the previous user's name and balance badge. Crash-free rate is unaffected; it shows up in about 0.02% of sessions (roughly 480 users/day have multiple accounts on one device). Logout clears the DB, tokens, and navigates to Login. The first login's network call is slow (p95 700 ms).
questions.promptHtml: Explain the leak mechanically, mitigate it, and fix it durably. Be specific about what you would and wouldn't do in the flow layer.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Clear the screen state on logout" or "recreate the ViewModel". Singleton replay cache survives ViewModels and the Activity; the weak answer doesn't find the actual store.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the repository process-scoped (singleton)? Does logout kill the process or just navigate? What else holds user data in memory (other replay caches, in-memory caches, stateIn results)? Is the leaked data PII under our compliance rules (yes, so severity high)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Gate behind a server-side flag/kill switch if the screen can hide the badge until a fresh load; ship a hotfix that calls profileFlow.resetReplayCache() on logout. Notify security with scope: only multi-account-on-one-process-lifetime users.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) replay cache in a singleton retains user A's Profile and replays it to user B's first subscriber; (b) Compose/ViewModel saved state restoring old data (unlikely: cleared on logout, and ViewModels recreate); (c) HTTP cache returning A's response (red herring: auth header differs and OkHttp cache keys include URL only, but responses are no-store); (d) Room not cleared (checked: cleared in a transaction).
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce: login A, logout, login B with a network throttle of 1.5 s; Home flashes A. Heap dump (Android Studio Profiler) after logout: MutableSharedFlow/SharedFlowImpl instance with buffer[0] = Profile(A) reachable from Hilt singleton. Log profile.replayCache at logout.
  5. Root cause: A replay cache lives as long as the flow object, not as long as a subscriber or session. Logout didn't touch it, and B's first collector got replay=1 = A's profile immediately, until B's network response replaced it.
  6. Fix: Short-term: _profile.resetReplayCache() in the logout handler (supported on SharedFlow; old subscribers keep buffered items but none exist after navigation). Long-term: make user-scoped state have a user-scoped lifetime. Options: (1) hold MutableStateFlow<ProfileState>(ProfileState.Empty) and reset to Empty on logout, since StateFlow can't reset its cache but a sentinel works; (2) scope the repository to a user-session component (Hilt custom component @UserScope recreated at login) so every cache dies with the session; (3) key data by userId and have the UI reject mismatching ids.
sealed interface ProfileState { data object Empty : ProfileState; data class Loaded(val userId: String, val p: Profile) : ProfileState }

class ProfileRepository @Inject constructor(...) {
    private val _profile = MutableStateFlow<ProfileState>(ProfileState.Empty)
    val profile: StateFlow<ProfileState> = _profile.asStateFlow()
    fun onLogout() { _profile.value = ProfileState.Empty }   // or: SharedFlow + resetReplayCache()
}
  1. Prevention: A "session teardown contract": every user-scoped holder implements SessionScoped.clear(), registered into a list invoked at logout; a unit test that logs in A, logs out, logs in B and asserts no value of A is ever collected. Heap-dump check in a QA script. Security review checklist: any replay, stateIn, LruCache, object singleton.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't kill the process on logout as the "fix" (brutal UX, still wrong on process reuse paths). I wouldn't rely on the UI to hide it for 700 ms with a spinner without clearing the data (data still in memory/heap). resetReplayCache() alone is fragile (forgettable); session-scoped DI is the structural fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not MutableStateFlow with resetReplayCache()? → It throws UnsupportedOperationException; reset by assigning an empty/sentinel value.
  • A slow collector from the old session is still attached with a buffered item? → resetReplayCache doesn't remove values already buffered for existing subscribers; make sure old collectors are cancelled (scope torn down) on logout.
  • What about stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5000, replayExpirationMillis = 0))? → That resets the replay to the initial value after the timeout when there are no subscribers; helps stale data but is time-based, not logout-based, so don't use it as a security control.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A similar leak was found in a news-feed app: a personalised "continue reading" row was served from a singleton replay cache. The fix that stuck wasn't the reset call; it was moving all user data into a session-scoped graph so it couldn't outlive the user by construction.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Looks only at UI/ViewModel, cannot locate the retention.
  • Hire: Identifies replay cache in singleton, calls resetReplayCache() or sentinel state on logout.
