  • Strong hire: Adds session-scoped DI, heap-dump verification, understands old-subscriber buffering caveat, treats it as a privacy incident with a prevention test.

questions.promptHtml: What happens when you apply distinctUntilChanged(), conflate(), flowOn(), map {} or catch {} to a StateFlow or SharedFlow? What does each return, and which are meaningless?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: People pile operators on StateFlow out of habit. Understanding which return types survive and which are no-ops shows you know hot vs cold and the "never completes" rule.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Operators like map or filter on a StateFlow return a plain Flow, not a StateFlow, so you lose .value and the hot-state type; the result is cold in the sense that each collector re-runs the operator chain on top of the shared source. Some operators are redundant on shared flows and are deprecated (error level) for that reason: distinctUntilChanged on StateFlow (already distinct), conflate/flowOn/cancellable on SharedFlow (no effect on the shared upstream). catch is meaningless on them in practice because a shared flow never completes with an exception from its own emission. If I need a StateFlow again after transforming, I use stateIn."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Type: fun <T, R> Flow<T>.map(...): returns Flow<R>. The operator wraps the source collect; each downstream collector subscribes to the shared source separately and runs the transform itself. So state.map { expensive(it) } collected by 3 collectors runs expensive 3 times per change.
  • Redundant: StateFlow is already distinctUntilChanged (by equals), already conflated, and its upstream context is the writer's. The library marks StateFlow.distinctUntilChanged(), SharedFlow.conflate(), SharedFlow.flowOn(), SharedFlow.cancellable() with @Deprecated(level = ERROR) pointing out they have no effect (since 1.6.0, I recall; verify against your version's Share.kt/docs).
  • Useful on StateFlow: map, filter, combine, flatMapLatest, distinctUntilChangedBy { it.field } (a different key than the whole-state equality is useful when you only care about one field of a big state), drop, onEach for side effects per collector.
  • Terminal: first(), first { predicate } work and return, e.g. await a condition. toList(), collect don't return.
  • catch/retry: source cannot throw into the flow; exceptions come from downstream operators you added, and catch can handle those upstream of itself. Not meaningless if you added a throwing map, but the shared source itself is infallible.
  • Re-sharing: to turn a derived Flow into a StateFlow: .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial). That does the transform once for all collectors.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _ui.asStateFlow()

val title: Flow<String> = state.map { it.title }              // plain Flow, no .value
val titleState: StateFlow<String> =                            // derived StateFlow, computed once
    state.map { it.title }.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), "")

state.distinctUntilChanged()            // compile error (deprecated ERROR): no effect
state.map { it.title }.distinctUntilChanged()   // fine: map output may repeat even if state changed

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• state.map {}.value: doesn't exist.
  • Doing heavy mapping in each collector instead of once with stateIn.
  • Adding .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) on a StateFlow collector chain: it only moves the downstream-of-source operators (above flowOn), not the collector.
  • distinctUntilChanged after map is useful and not redundant; blanket removal breaks that.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is distinctUntilChanged() error-deprecated on StateFlow but not after map? → The result of map is a plain Flow whose values aren't guaranteed distinct.
  2. collectAsStateWithLifecycle on a derived Flow? → Needs an initialValue; a StateFlow doesn't.
  3. Is combine(stateA, stateB) conflation-safe? → Each input is conflated; combine emits on any input change; see Q530 for torn-state.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "you can use map/filter on it". Senior notes return types, per-collector re-execution of the chain, redundant/deprecated operators, and stateIn to re-share.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A state.map { toUiModels(it) } (5 ms, 3 collectors including a bottom sheet) tripled main-thread work per update; moving it to a stateIn in the ViewModel with Dispatchers.Default upstream fixed jank.

questions.contextHtml: A trading app's price ticker uses a PriceBus singleton: MutableSharedFlow<Tick>(extraBufferCapacity = 8) (default SUSPEND). A WebSocket reader coroutine on Dispatchers.IO calls bus.emit(tick) for each message. Three collectors: a Compose list (cheap, 0.3 ms/tick), a mini-chart on Main (8 ms/tick drawing), and a Room writer (3 ms/tick, batched off-main). With 40 symbols the feed is about 150 ticks/s and is fine. The company adds 400 symbols for premium: about 1,500 ticks/s. After rollout: socket disconnects with "ping timeout" every ~40 s, ANR rate rises from 0.2% to 0.9%, battery drain complaints. Server says the client stops reading from the socket.
questions.promptHtml: Why does a 10x increase cause disconnects and ANRs, and how do you redesign the bus?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the buffer capacity." At 1,500/s with an 8 ms chart, any finite buffer fills in seconds; and "switch the socket to a bigger thread pool" doesn't address backpressure.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which consumers need every tick (Room writer for history?) vs only the latest per symbol (UI)? Is order per symbol required? What's the acceptable staleness (say 100-250 ms)? Do all 440 symbols show at once?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side/feature flag to reduce subscribed symbols; client hotfix: change the bus to DROP_OLDEST so the socket reader never blocks.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) SUSPEND policy: the reader's emit waits for the slowest subscriber (chart at 8 ms/tick = max 125 ticks/s) so the reader is throttled to 125/s < 1,500/s, stops reading, TCP window fills, server pings time out; (b) main-thread saturation: 1,500 ticks/s x 8 ms = 12 s of work per second, so Main is permanently busy -> ANR; (c) memory growth from unbounded waiting emitters (if emit is called from multiple coroutines); (d) battery from constant redraw (symptom, not cause).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto/system trace: Main thread 100% busy with chart draw; WebSocket reader thread blocked in emit (coroutine dump or DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() shows suspended in SharedFlowImpl.emit); measure ticks/s in vs ticks/s processed per collector; OkHttp logs for ping timeouts; ANR traces in Play Console.
  5. Root cause: Math: chart capacity = 1000 ms / 8 ms = 125 ticks/s; arrival = 1,500 ticks/s; deficit = 1,375 ticks/s. With SUSPEND, backpressure propagates all the way to the socket read; the slowest subscriber sets the speed for everyone, including the Room writer. Separately, the chart does 12x more drawing than frames the display can show (60 fps = 16.7 ms frames).
  6. Fix: Separate "must process all" from "latest is enough":
    • Socket reader: never blocks; push into a per-symbol latest-value store (ConcurrentHashMap<Symbol, Tick> / MutableStateFlow<Map> updated by update), plus a Channel(UNLIMITED/BUFFERED) into a batching writer for history (chunked by time/size, off-main).
    • UI: sample at frame rate: ticksFlow.sample(100) (or a 16-33 ms ticker reading latest snapshot), 10 UI updates/s instead of 1,500.
    • Bus config for any remaining broadcast: MutableSharedFlow<Tick>(extraBufferCapacity = 256, onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST); each consumer adds its own .buffer/.conflate() as appropriate.
private val _ticks = MutableSharedFlow<Tick>(extraBufferCapacity = 256, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)
val ticks: SharedFlow<Tick> = _ticks.asSharedFlow()

val uiTicks: Flow<Map<Symbol, Tick>> = latestBySymbol.sample(100)   // 10 Hz, latest snapshot
  1. Prevention: Load test with a replay of a recorded 3,000 ticks/s feed in CI (macrobenchmark + frame timing); metric: reader thread blocked time; alert on ANR rate; code-review rule: any hot-path emit into SUSPEND needs a documented slowest-consumer analysis.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: DROP_OLDEST drops ticks: fine for UI, not for history (hence the separate lossless path). I wouldn't use Channel(UNLIMITED) for the UI path (unbounded memory: 1,500 x ~100 B = 150 KB/s growth, 9 MB/min while Main is blocked). I wouldn't move the chart draw to Default (drawing must be on Main; reduce the work instead).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if regulators require every tick persisted? → Lossless path with a bounded channel + disk batching + explicit backpressure to the socket via TCP flow control, and a sequence-number gap detector.
  • Why not conflate() on each collector instead? → On a SharedFlow, per-collector .conflate() is allowed on the collector side (it adds a buffer between the shared flow and your collector) but the emitter still sees SUSPEND until that buffer accepts; with conflate it always accepts, so it works for the UI path.
  • Does StateFlow per symbol fit? → 440 StateFlows is fine memory-wise; a map-snapshot or SnapshotStateMap is simpler.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An IoT dashboard shipped fine in beta (50 devices). With 800 devices the websocket thread was blocked by a single slow subscriber, the broker dropped the client, and reconnect storms followed. The root fix was not capacity tuning but classifying every subscriber as lossless or latest-only.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Increases buffer or threads.
  • Hire: Identifies SUSPEND backpressure to the socket and uses DROP_OLDEST/sample/conflate.
  • Strong hire: Does the math (125/s vs 1,500/s; 12 s of work per second), splits lossless vs latest-only paths, and adds replay-load testing and thread-blocked metrics.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through replayCache and resetReplayCache(): what exactly do new and existing subscribers see, how does it differ for StateFlow, and where does replay become a liability?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Replay is the source of both "lost event" fixes and "stale event" bugs. Senior engineers know both edges.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "replayCache is a read-only snapshot of the last replay values that a new subscriber will receive first. resetReplayCache() empties it: new subscribers get only values emitted afterwards, but subscribers already attached still receive values already buffered for them. On StateFlow the replay cache is always exactly the current value and resetReplayCache() throws UnsupportedOperationException, so you reset state by writing a sentinel value. Replay is a liability when the value is an event (it replays on every resubscribe, like after rotation or repeatOnLifecycle restarts), when it holds user-scoped data that outlives a session, and when it keeps large objects alive."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Replay cache = the last min(replay, emitted) values, retained even with zero subscribers (this is the only thing retained without subscribers).
  • New subscriber start index = start of the replay window. So subscribing yields replayCache items in order, then live ones. Not atomic with respect to emissions: the library guarantees no gaps between the replay and live values for that subscriber.
  • resetReplayCache(): documented as "new subscribers receive only the values emitted after this call, old subscribers still receive previously buffered values". It's not a "clear everything".
  • On MutableSharedFlow with replay = 0, resetReplayCache() is a no-op.
  • StateFlow.replayCache = listOf(value). MutableStateFlow.resetReplayCache() throws UnsupportedOperationException("MutableStateFlow.resetReplayCache is not supported") because a StateFlow must always have a value.
  • Lifecycle interplay: repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) cancels and re-collects, a fresh subscription every time -> replay delivered every time. For states that's desired; for events (navigate, show snackbar) it duplicates (see next chunk).
  • shareIn(scope, started, replay) and stateIn have SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis, replayExpirationMillis): after the timeout with no subscribers, the shared flow stops the upstream; after replayExpirationMillis the replay cache is reset (for stateIn, back to initialValue). Default replayExpirationMillis = Long.MAX_VALUE = never expires: stale data stays.
  • Memory: replay=N keeps N objects strongly reachable as long as the flow object lives (singleton = process lifetime).
Use case Replay?
Current user, settings, "latest config" StateFlow or replay=1
Navigation/snackbar events No replay (or consume-once state); replay=1 re-fires
Late subscriber needs last N log lines replay=N, bounded N
User-scoped data in singleton replay only with session teardown (Q525)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val sh = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(replay = 2)
sh.tryEmit(1); sh.tryEmit(2); sh.tryEmit(3)
println(sh.replayCache)        // [2, 3]
sh.resetReplayCache()
println(sh.replayCache)        // []

val st = MutableStateFlow("a")
st.replayCache                 // ["a"]
// st.resetReplayCache()       // UnsupportedOperationException

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming reset also removes values pending for live subscribers.
  • Reading replayCache.last() on possibly empty cache (NoSuchElementException); use lastOrNull().
  • Using replay as a delivery guarantee for events.
  • Forgetting that replayCache is a snapshot; it's stale the moment you read it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can replay be large and cheap? → It's a circular buffer; cost is retained memory, not CPU. Keep it bounded by value size.
  2. How would you implement "replay latest but not after consumption"? → That's a consume-once pattern: a Channel or state with an event id and consumed() callback.
  3. Replay and distinctUntilChanged on the consumer? → Applies to the combined replay+live stream seen by that collector, not to the shared cache.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "replay gives new subscribers the last values". Senior covers the exact reset semantics, StateFlow's difference, lifecycle resubscription replays, expiration in WhileSubscribed, and memory/security retention.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feature-flag SharedFlow with replay = 1 in a singleton kept replaying a large remote-config blob after logout; a heap dump showed a 3 MB object pinned for the process lifetime.

questions.contextHtml: A 6-year-old codebase has a helper used in 40 ViewModels: fun <T> stateLike() = MutableSharedFlow<T>(replay = 1, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST), because "StateFlow didn't allow no-initial-value". Compose screens read .replayCache.lastOrNull() in places. Plan: migrate to MutableStateFlow across the board, 3.1M DAU, staged rollout 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over two weeks. Known risks: unit tests, analytics, some screens call resetReplayCache() on logout.
questions.promptHtml: What changes behaviorally between the two, which of those can bite you in prod, and how do you execute the migration safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Search and replace the type; add a default value." Misses dedupe, resetReplayCache crash, null-vs-empty semantics, and analytics shifts.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screens depend on "no value yet" (spinner) vs an empty default? Do any collectors rely on repeated identical emissions (refresh, retry)? Which code calls resetReplayCache()? Are there collectors that count or log emissions? Do tests assert on duplicates?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed (planned). Use the rollout gates and a kill switch via a wrapper factory so we can revert type per screen.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (what will differ): (a) resetReplayCache() throws UnsupportedOperationException on MutableStateFlow at runtime (logout crash!); (b) equal consecutive values no longer emitted: refresh-by-re-emitting breaks, impressions/analytics counts drop; (c) initial value now exists: collectors see a default first (flash of empty UI, or a skipped loading state); (d) replayCache.lastOrNull() call sites still compile (StateFlow has replayCache) but now never null; semantics change silently; (e) emit from Dispatchers.Default fine, but code using replayCache + emit non-atomically should move to update.
  4. How I'd verify each: Grep/detekt for resetReplayCache, replayCache, tryEmit, emit in the 40 VMs; tests with Turbine asserting duplicate sequences; analytics event counts per screen during canary vs control (should drop only where duplicates existed); crash dashboards filtered by UnsupportedOperationException; screenshot tests for initial-state frames.
  5. Root cause of the risk: The two types look interchangeable but encode different contracts (Q522): state with distinct/atomic updates vs a stream with replay.
  6. Fix (plan):
    • Introduce StateHolder<T> factory returning MutableStateFlow with an explicit sealed UiState initial (Loading), per screen, replacing null meaning "not loaded".
    • Replace resetReplayCache() with value = Initial (logout handled via session scope, Q525).
    • Replace replayCache.last() with .value, and read-modify-write with update {}.
    • For the few places needing duplicates (explicit refresh), add a refreshTick field or a separate event flow.
    • Migrate in small PRs per ViewModel, behind a debug-only assertion wrapper that logs when value = x is ignored as equal in canary builds, to find hidden reliance on duplicates.
    • Rollout: ship per batch of ViewModels, compare screen-level analytics counts, crash-free sessions, and first-frame render time at 1%/10% before widening.
  7. Prevention: Lint rule banning MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1, DROP_OLDEST) in ViewModels; docs in the architecture guide: "state -> StateFlow, events -> separate mechanism"; tests using runTest + Turbine for each state holder.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't do a repo-wide mechanical rewrite in one release (risk concentration, unattributable regressions). I wouldn't keep the old helper "just in case" indefinitely (two ways to do state). I wouldn't introduce nullable StateFlow everywhere as a shortcut to keep "no value": that pushes null-handling into every screen.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Analytics impressions dropped 6% on a screen after migration; is that a regression? → Likely previously over-counted duplicates; confirm against server-side events and deduped logs before reverting.
  • A collector depended on seeing "same value again" to re-trigger a scroll-to-top. → That's an event masquerading as state; add an explicit event or counter.
  • Could you keep SharedFlow and fix the problems instead? → For screens needing "no value" semantics and duplicates, yes; the choice is per use case.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration like this crashed ~0.3% of sessions at logout in the first canary because one ViewModel still called resetReplayCache() through a shared base class. The staged rollout limited blast radius; the dashboard filter on UnsupportedOperationException caught it in under an hour.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Mechanical type swap without behavior analysis.
  • Hire: Lists dedupe, initial value, resetReplayCache exception and plans staged rollout.
  • Strong hire: Adds assertion instrumentation for ignored equal writes, analytics baseline comparison, event-vs-state split, and prevention via lint and conventions.

questions.contextHtml:
A marketplace search screen (1.8M DAU) shows a spinner, results, or an empty-state ("No results"). The ViewModel keeps two flows and combines them for the UI:

private val _loading = MutableStateFlow(false)
private val _results = MutableStateFlow<List<Item>>(emptyList())

val ui: StateFlow<Ui> = combine(_loading, _results) { loading, items ->
    when {
        loading -> Ui.Spinner
        items.isEmpty() -> Ui.Empty
        else -> Ui.Content(items)
    }
}.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), Ui.Spinner)

fun search(q: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
    _loading.value = true
    val r = repo.search(q)
    _loading.value = false      // (A)
    _results.value = r          // (B)
}

Post-incident: ~4% of searches flash "No results" for 1-2 frames before the real list on mid-range devices; a screenshot-test flaked once; QA also saw the empty state flash with a spinner skipped under heavy load. The team first "fixed" it by adding delay(16) between (A) and (B), which reduced but didn't remove it.
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident review: cause, why the delay "worked" partially, the fix, and what you'd change in team practice.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Swap the order of (A) and (B)" (just moves the flash to old results shown after loading), or "use debounce". Neither addresses non-atomic multi-flow state.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the flash only on search completion or also on first load? Does the old result list persist between searches (stale content shown on a new query is fine)? Do all writes happen on Main? Does the same pattern exist elsewhere?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the delay(16) hack; temporary swap to set results before clearing loading (B then A) which at least avoids the false "empty" while the real fix is prepared. Honest note: that can show stale items for a frame.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) two independent StateFlows are updated by two separate writes; combine can emit between them with loading=false, items=emptyList() -> Empty; (b) combine conflation/dispatching on Main: when the collector is slower, it may observe the (A)-then-(B) states, or only the combined final state, causing the intermittence; (c) stateIn replay of an old combined value (red herring: initial Spinner is right); (d) repo.search returning empty first (red herring: payload logs show non-empty).
  4. How I'd verify each: A Turbine test: collect ui, call search, assert the emission sequence; it fails with Spinner, Empty, Content. Reproduce under StandardTestDispatcher vs UnconfinedTestDispatcher to show it's timing/dispatch dependent. Compose recomposition trace or log in the combine lambda with timestamps.
  5. Root cause: Two StateFlows can't be updated atomically together. State = (loading, items) is one logical state. combine is built to react to each input change independently and does not know that (A) and (B) belong together. Whether the collector sees the intermediate (false, []) depends on dispatch timing, hence 4% on slow devices, and why delay(16) shrinks but cannot eliminate the window (it only makes it likelier that a frame boundary falls between, i.e. it can make it worse for another timing).
  6. Fix: One immutable state object and one atomic write:
data class SearchState(val loading: Boolean = false, val items: List<Item> = emptyList(), val searched: Boolean = false)

private val _state = MutableStateFlow(SearchState())
val ui: StateFlow<SearchState> = _state.asStateFlow()

fun search(q: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
    _state.update { it.copy(loading = true) }
    val r = repo.search(q)
    _state.update { SearchState(loading = false, items = r, searched = true) }   // single atomic transition
}

Map SearchState to Spinner/Empty/Content at the edge (when in UI or a pure toUi()), with Empty only when searched && !loading && items.isEmpty(). Also handle cancellation of the previous search (flatMapLatest or cancel the previous Job). 7. Prevention: Convention: "one screen, one state object, transitions via update". Reviewer red flag: combine of StateFlows that are written by the same function. Turbine tests asserting the exact emission sequence for each user action. Add a screenshot test with StandardTestDispatcher to catch intermediate states. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't add delays/debounce to mask the window (nondeterministic, adds latency to every search). I wouldn't use Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot-style trickery to batch two flows; it doesn't apply to flows. combine is fine when inputs are genuinely independent (e.g. user prefs + network state).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Single state object but 8 independent sub-states updated by different parts? → Compose a state from independent sources via combine in one place, but writes that must be consistent go through one flow.
  • Doesn't one big state cause extra recomposition? → Use stable/immutable classes and derive slices with distinctUntilChangedBy/derivedStateOf; measure before splitting.
  • Would zip help? → No; it pairs by emission count, not by logical state.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "flaky" screenshot test was quarantined for months; the real defect was this combine pattern, and it also produced a user-visible flicker on lower-end phones. The deciding clue was that the test passed on Unconfined dispatchers and failed on Standard.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Reorders statements or adds delay/debounce.
  • Hire: Identifies non-atomic two-flow state and merges into one state with update.
  • Strong hire: Explains dispatch-dependent intermittence, adds sequence-asserting tests under both test dispatchers, handles search cancellation, and sets team conventions about when combine is appropriate.
